subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How many atmospheric circulation cells operate in each hemisphere in the global circulation model?
questions.explain: Each hemisphere has three cells: the Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells.

questions.q: Which circulation cell lies closest to the equator?
questions.explain: The Hadley cell operates between the equator and about 30 degrees latitude.

questions.q: Why do many of the world's major hot deserts form at around 30 degrees north and south?
options: Rising warm air produces heavy rainfall
Sinking air creates high pressure and dry conditions
Cold ocean currents cool the land
questions.explain: At about 30 degrees, air descending in the Hadley cell forms high pressure, giving dry, cloud-free conditions.

questions.q: What is the approximate minimum sea-surface temperature needed for a tropical storm to form?
questions.explain: Tropical storms need warm ocean water of at least about 27 degrees Celsius to supply energy.

questions.q: Why do tropical storms rarely form exactly on the equator?
options: The sea is too cold there
The Coriolis effect is too weak to make storms spin
There is too little water vapour
Air pressure is always very high
questions.explain: The Coriolis effect, which gives storms their spin, is negligible within about 5 degrees of the equator.

questions.q: Which best describes the conditions experienced in the eye of a tropical storm?
options: The strongest winds and heaviest rain
Calm, clear skies with low pressure
questions.explain: In the eye, air is descending, producing calm, clear and dry conditions despite the surrounding storm.

questions.q: What name is given to tropical storms that form in the western Pacific Ocean?
questions.explain: The same type of storm is called a typhoon in the western Pacific, a hurricane in the Atlantic and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: A region of ocean has a surface temperature of 23 degrees Celsius and warm water only to a depth of 30 metres. A tropical storm is unlikely to form here mainly because:
options: The water is not warm or deep enough to supply energy
The Coriolis effect is too strong
There is too much water vapour
The air pressure is too low
questions.explain: Storms need warm water of about 27 degrees to roughly 70 metres depth, so 23 degrees to 30 metres is insufficient.

questions.q: What is the main source of energy that powers a tropical storm?
options: Latent heat released as water vapour condenses
questions.explain: Evaporation from the warm ocean supplies moisture, and latent heat released as it condenses drives the storm.

questions.q: Which layer of the Earth is liquid?
questions.explain: The outer core is a liquid layer of iron and nickel, while the inner core is solid.

questions.q: What is the main process that causes tectonic plates to move?
questions.explain: Heat from the core drives convection currents in the mantle that move the plates above.

questions.q: At which type of plate boundary do two plates move towards each other?
questions.explain: At a destructive (convergent) boundary plates move together, often with oceanic crust subducting beneath continental crust.

questions.q: What happens at a constructive plate boundary such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
options: Plates move apart and new crust is formed
Plates collide to form fold mountains
questions.explain: At a constructive boundary plates diverge and rising magma creates new crust.

questions.q: Two continental plates move towards each other but neither can sink because both are low density. What is most likely to form?
questions.explain: At a collision boundary neither plate subducts, so crust is forced upwards into fold mountains such as the Himalayas.

questions.q: What is the name for the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake?
questions.explain: The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus, where the earthquake originates underground.

questions.q: Why do conservative (transform) plate boundaries produce earthquakes but not volcanoes?
options: The plates are too cold to melt
No magma reaches the surface because crust is neither created nor destroyed
They are always found under the sea
questions.explain: Plates slide past each other, so no crust is made or lost and no magma rises, but friction still causes earthquakes.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to detect and measure earthquakes?
questions.explain: A seismometer records the ground shaking produced by an earthquake.

questions.q: Designing buildings with cross-bracing and deep foundations to withstand shaking is an example of which hazard management approach?
questions.explain: Earthquake-resistant design is protection, aiming to reduce damage and deaths when an event occurs.

questions.q: A city on a fault line cannot stop earthquakes happening. Which strategy would most reduce loss of life?
options: Preparation through drills, education and emergency planning
Ignoring the risk to save money
questions.explain: Since earthquakes cannot be prevented, preparation such as drills and planning helps people respond and survive.
